items.readable_text:
Content:
We can use the standard algorithm to multiply a three-digit number by a one-digit number. In this case, we might need to carry a digit from the multiplication of the ones and tens.

Content:
For instance, let's find the value of

Content:
[MATH: 143 \times 7.]

Content:
We start by writing the problem out as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 1|4|3; ×|7|10and2 + 10 = 1200000]

Content:
First, we multiply the ones. We have [MATH: 3\times 7 = {\color{blue}2}{\color{red}1}.] We write [MATH: \color{red}1] in the ones place and carry the [MATH: {\color{blue}2}.]

Content:
[MATH: _(2); 1|4|3; ×|7; 1|3 × 7 = 2100000000000000000; Carry:2; Write:1]

Content:
Next, we multiply the tens as follows:

Content:
- We have [MATH: 4\times 7= 28.]
- We add the [MATH: 2] carried from the previous multiplication to get [MATH: 2+28 = {\color{blue}3}{\color{red}0}.]
- We write down [MATH: \color{red}0] and carry [MATH: {\color{blue}3}.]

Content:
[MATH: _(3)|_(2); 1|4|3; ×|7; 0|1|4 × 7 = 28and2 + 28 = 30; Carry:3; Write:0]

Content:
Finally, we multiply the hundreds as follows:

Content:
- We have [MATH: 1\times 7 = 7.]
- We add the [MATH: 3] carried from the previous multiplication to get [MATH: 3+7= 10.]
- Since this is the final multiplication, we write the entire result, [MATH: {\color{red}10}.]

Content:
[MATH: _(3)|_(2); 1|4|3; ×|7; 1|0|0|1|1 × 7 = 7and3 + 7 = 10; Carry:−; Write:10]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: 143 \times 7 = 1,001.]

[MATH: _(2); 2|1|6|2; ×|4; 6|4|8|1 × 4 = 4and2 + 4 = 6; Carry: −; Write:6]

Finally, we multiply the thousands:

[MATH: _(2); 2|1|6|2; ×|4; 8|6|4|8|2 × 4 = 80000000000000000; Carry:−; Write:8]
